title: Trump: Ivanka Trump applies for Chinese trademark on voting machines
description_short: Trump: Ivanka Trump applies for Chinese trademark on voting machines
description_medium: Ivanka Trump applied for 16 Chinese trademarks in May 2016, including one covering voting machines. The filings were part of a broader set of applications made between March and May for varied goods and services. The available account describes applications, not proof that products were manufactured or sold.
description_long: Ivanka Trump submitted applications for 16 Chinese trademarks in May 2016, including one covering voting machines. The filings were part of dozens of applications made between March and May for goods and services ranging from hospitals and nursing homes to cameras, lottery machines, and industrial equipment. An application is a request for trademark protection; it does not establish that the mark was granted or that a product entered the market. The available account does not provide registry records, ownership details, or the disposition of the applications. Because the filings predated the 2016 election, this summary does not establish that they overlapped with a government role or influenced public policy. The application records and later trademark status are needed to determine what rights, if any, were granted and how the marks were used.

title: Donald Trump buys Mar-a-Lago after months of lies and media coverage
description_short: Donald Trump buys Mar-a-Lago after months of lies and media coverage
description_medium: Donald Trump acquired Mar-a-Lago, a 17-acre Palm Beach estate with a large Mediterranean-style mansion, in 1985. In his memoir, Trump said he first heard about the property at dinner, toured it, and bought it. The account does not specify which earlier statements or media coverage were allegedly false.
description_long: Donald Trump acquired Mar-a-Lago, a 17-acre Palm Beach estate with a large Mediterranean-style mansion, in 1985. In The Art of the Comeback, Trump recounted hearing about the property during dinner, touring it, and then buying it. That account of how he found the estate comes from his memoir. The headline says the purchase followed months of lies and media coverage, but the available details do not identify the statements alleged to be false or show how publicity affected the sale. The purchase price, negotiation terms, and seller’s account are also not provided. The documented event is the acquisition; the claim that deception or media coverage drove the transaction requires examples and evidence. The available facts do not establish that Trump planned Mar-a-Lago’s later role when he bought the property. No seller account or contemporaneous documentation is included to corroborate the memoir’s version.

title: Trump World Tower opens, uses mafia to sell condos to Russia
description_short: Trump World Tower opens, uses mafia to sell condos to Russia
description_medium: Trump World Tower opened in Manhattan in early 2001. The supplied account reports that at least 65 units were sold to Russian buyers by the end of 2004 and that Saudi Arabia bought the entire 45th floor for $4.5 million. The title’s claims about criminal financing and mafia sales are not established by those figures.
description_long: Trump World Tower, a Manhattan condominium development, opened in early 2001. The account reports that at least 65 units were sold to Russian buyers between construction and the end of 2004 and that Saudi Arabia bought the entire 45th floor for $4.5 million. Bloomberg’s investigation examined Russian buyers and wealthy occupants associated with the building. The headline alleges that a mafia organization helped sell units and that criminal banks financed the project, but the available details do not name those banks, establish criminal findings, or describe a sales arrangement involving organized crime. The buyer count also needs underlying records. Nationality and wealth do not establish criminal conduct, and ownership in the building does not show that a buyer influenced Trump’s later political decisions. Documentation for the financing and sales allegations is needed.

title: Trump: Daily Beast releases fluff piece on Jeffrey Epstein, featuring Wilbur Ross
description_short: Trump: Daily Beast releases fluff piece on Jeffrey Epstein, featuring Wilbur Ross
description_medium: The Daily Beast published an April 2011 article by Alexandra Wolfe featuring New York figures discussing Jeffrey Epstein, including Wilbur Ross. The archive criticizes the article’s treatment of Epstein’s victims, but the relevant text and quotations are not included. Ross’s presence in the article does not by itself show he endorsed its framing.
description_long: The Daily Beast published an article by Alexandra Wolfe in April 2011 that included comments from New York figures about Jeffrey Epstein, among them Wilbur Ross, who later became Trump’s commerce secretary. The archive criticizes the article as flattering Epstein and says it portrayed underage victims as troublemakers. Those claims concern the piece’s framing, but the available excerpt does not include the text, relevant quotations, or their context. A person quoted in a profile is not thereby shown to have endorsed Epstein or the article’s treatment of survivors. The article and passages supporting the criticism are needed to assess how it represented the victims. Ross’s later government service is also separate from his appearance in the 2011 story; no connection between the two is established.
